extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/practitioners referencing examiner practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and rejecting patent claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) and related claim-drafting issues, including appropriate use of form paragraphs, examples, and prosecution practice to avoid piecemeal examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Gustafson and In re Collier. If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by the specification, consider MPEP § 2172.01. Do not rely on a non‑statutory 'aggregation' rejection; identify the correct statutory basis (35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, or 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolix
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should reject claims as prolix only when long recitations or unimportant details render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are prolix when the metes and bounds of the claimed subject matter cannot be determined due to long, unnecessary recitations. Reject as prolix only in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one claim may be presented provided they differ substantially and are not unduly multiplied; unduly multiplied or repetitious claims may be rejected as undue multiplicity under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.75. Apply the 'rule of reason'—allow reasonable latitude but reject repetition that beclouds definition. Undue multiplicity rejections should be rare and applied judiciously. Examiner should contact applicant by telephone to request selection of claims for examination; if applicant refuses, make undue multiplicity rejection in next Office action and request applicant's selection in reply. Preserves right to PTAB review. Also note Ex parte Whitelaw/Ex parte Kochan doctrines for duplicate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double Inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se rule that 'double inclusion' is improper in a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate facts of each case to determine whether multiple inclusion of one or more elements leads to indefiniteness. Multiple inclusion in Markush groups does not necessarily create uncertainty; but where a device claim can be read to include the same element twice, the claim may be indefinite. Apply precedent (e.g., In re Kelly, Ex parte Kristensen) with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Directed to Product-By-Process or Product and Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may permissively reference more than one statutory class. A product-by-process claim (product defined by process) is proper; by contrast a single claim claiming both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I. PRODUCT‑BY‑PROCESS: Product claims defined in terms of process are proper if clearly directed to the product (cases: Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma; In re Luck; In re Pilkington; In re Steppan). Applicants may present claims of varying scope even if product must be described product‑by‑process. II. PRODUCT AND PROCESS IN THE SAME CLAIM: A claim that recites a product and actions by users (method steps) may be indefinite (e.g., In re Katz). If additional limitations focus on system capabilities (not user actions), claim may be definite (Mastermine Software v. Microsoft).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Use" Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that attempt to claim a process without setting forth steps (mere 'use' claims) generally raise indefiniteness issues under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and may fail 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim reciting a 'process for using X to isolate Y' held indefinite for reciting only a use without active steps (Ex parte Erlich). 'Use' claims that do not purport to be a statutory class fail 101 (In re Moreton). It may be appropriate to reject under both 101 and 112(b) if facts support both. However, some claims reciting 'utilizing' have been held not indefinite (Ex parte Porter). When rejecting, use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.01, 7.34.01) as indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph) as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail to point out what is included or excluded. Use form paragraph 7.35 to effect rejection; see Ex parte Fressola for history and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Figures or Tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should, where possible, be complete in themselves; incorporation by reference to a figure or table is permitted only in exceptional circumstances where there is no practical way to define the invention in words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporation by reference is a 'necessity' doctrine, not for applicant convenience (Ex parte Fressola). Reference characters may be used in claims alongside recitation of elements; generally their presence/absence does not affect claim scope. See MPEP § 608.01(m) for treatment of reference characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical Formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical structures in claims should not be considered indefinite nor speculative in the absence of evidence that the assigned formula is in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of corroborating spectroscopic or other data is not a basis for indefiniteness (Ex parte Morton; Ex parte Sobin). A chemical compound claim is not indefinite merely because structure is partial or not presented (In re Fisher). Compounds can be claimed by adequate names, combinations of physical/chemical characteristics, or by process of making without raising indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks or Trade Names in a Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper, but the claim should be carefully analyzed to determine how the mark or name is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademarks identify source and do not define goods; using a trademark as a limitation to describe a material/product fails 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (Ex parte Simpson). If applicant substitutes a generic term in response, examiner should determine whether sufficient support exists in the application for that generic term (see MPEP § 2163 II.A.3(b)). If a mark's presence causes confusion as to claim scope, reject under 112(b). Case example: Eli Lilly & Co. v. Apotex discussed handling of trade name 'ALIMTA'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Function of Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Process/method claims should not be rejected solely on the ground that they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Tarczy‑Hornoch: a process claim otherwise patentable should not be rejected merely because the application discloses an apparatus that will inherently carry out the recited steps. Do not use inherent machine function as sole basis for 112(b) rejection of process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Compact Prosecution: Interpret the Claim and Apply Art with Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under compact prosecution, examiners should identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action and clearly articulate any rejection early so applicant can reply completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should review each claim for compliance with all statutory requirements (37 CFR 1.104(a)(1)). When a claim term renders the claim indefinite, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and also make rejection(s) over prior art (35 U.S.C. 102/103) based on examiner's interpretation — state on the record how the term is being interpreted. Reject each claim on all valid grounds available to avoid piecemeal examination (see MPEP § 707.07(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Compact Prosecution: Prior Art Rejection of Claim Rejected as Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: All words in a claim must be considered when judging patentability against prior art; indefinite terms do not automatically make a claim obvious over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two approaches: (1) If uncertainty is not great and at least one interpretation renders the claim unpatentable, enter both an indefiniteness rejection under 112(b) and a prior art rejection based on the interpretation that makes it unpatentable (identify how claim is being interpreted); (2) If confusion is great, do not reject on prior art (avoid speculation per In re Steele). The first approach is recommended to avoid piecemeal examination and to help applicant redraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship Between the Requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enabling) and 112(b) (indefiniteness) are separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification is not commensurate in scope with the claim, that indicates insufficient disclosure under 112(a) (not necessarily indefiniteness under 112(b)). If the specification shows a feature is critical/essential and claim fails to recite it, a 112(a) rejection may be appropriate (In re Mayhew). If claim is amended to include subject matter not described in the application as filed, a 112(a) new matter rejection may be appropriate (In re Simon, In re Panagrossi).

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.30.02 Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph quoting 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph, to be used as statutory basis statement in Office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute quotation provided. Examiner notes: statute need not be re‑cited in all Office actions—required in first actions on the merits and final rejections; where statute not cited use paragraph 7.103. Paragraphs 7.30.01/7.30.02 used only once per Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34 Rejection, Failure To Claim Inventor's Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph) as failing to set forth the subject matter which the inventor/applicant regards as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when inventor/applicant has stated outside the application that the invention is different than claimed. In bracketed text identify the submission, the inventor's statement, and how it indicates a different invention. Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.01 Rejection, Failure To Particularly Point out and Distinctly Claim (Indefinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for rejecting claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Insert appropriate claim numbers and check dependent claims for same reason. Follow with applicable sub‑form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.10, 7.34.23–7.34.24, or provide a full explanation identifying particular indefinite terms/limitations. If person skilled in the art can determine scope, do not use this rejection. See MPEP §§ 2171–2174 for guidance; form paragraph 7.34.15 for pro se applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.02 Terminology Used Inconsistent with Accepted Meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for when applicant defines a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning without clearly redefining it in the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the applicant-assigned meaning and the accepted meaning (support accepted meaning via textbook/dictionary citation per MPEP § 2173.05(a)). This paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01. Examiner notes instruct how to populate brackets and provide support.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.03 Relative Term - Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for when a relative term or term of degree (e.g., 'sufficient', 'substantial') renders the claim indefinite because specification provides no standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain which parameter/quantity/limitation is rendered indefinite. Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.04 Broader Range/Limitation And Narrow Range/Limitation in Same Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for when a broad recitation and a narrower recitation that falls within it appear in the same claim, potentially rendering the claim indefinite regarding whether the narrower feature is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert the broad recitation and the narrower statement into brackets. This paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.05 Lack of Antecedent Basis in the Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for when a claim recites a limitation without sufficient antecedent basis (e.g., 'said lever' without prior mention of 'a lever').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes scope indeterminate. Provide location in claim where limitation appears. Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.07 Claims Are a Literal Translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for claims that are narrative, indefinite, and appear to be literal translations with grammatical/idiomatic errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the specification does not clearly redefine the claim term at issue. Precede with 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.08 Indefinite Claim Language: 'For Example'
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph noting that the phrase 'for example' renders a claim indefinite because it is unclear whether following limitations are part of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.09 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Or The Like'
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph advising that the phrase 'or the like' renders claims indefinite because elements encompassed by this phrase may not be disclosed and make scope unascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.10 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Such As'
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for the phrase 'such as' which renders a claim indefinite because it is unclear whether limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.12 Essential Steps Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph rejecting a method/process claim as incomplete for omitting essential steps, creating a gap between steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List omitted steps in bracket. Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. See MPEP § 2172.01 for guidance on omitted essential matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.34.15 Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112, Pro Se
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph tailored for pro se applicants addressing particular indefinite phrases (e.g., 'such as') that render claims indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. Use wording appropriate for pro se applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.35 Rejection, Failure To Particularly Point out and Distinctly Claim - Omnibus Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph for rejecting an omnibus type claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it fails to point out what is included/excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Use this paragraph to reject 'omnibus' claims; no further explanation necessary. Example omnibus claim: 'A device substantially as shown and described.'

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.35.01 Trademark or Trade Name as a Limitation in the Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph addressing use of trademark or trade name as a limitation in a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use where a trademark/trade name appears as a limiting term in a claim. If intended not as a limitation, examiner should question why it is present; if it causes confusion, reject under 112(b). See MPEP § 2163 for follow-up if applicant replaces with generic term.
